extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists/short-story writers), editors, literary readers interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and observations (in comic-essay form) about how novelists and short-story writers describe characters, structure episodes, and avoid wasteful or formulaic writing. Emphasizes economy, reader-projection, and awareness of publishing/serial constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of description / condenseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Nowadays we content ourselves—and our readers also, I am inclined to think—with dashing her off in a few bold strokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer short, vivid strokes over long catalogues of detail. The author contrasts past long-form character-builders with modern practice of sketching a heroine in a phrase or two; anti-patterns include wasting pages on slowly building a child’s backstory when a short synopsis could convey the plot. Examples: the sub-editor's condensed summaries that render whole chapters unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness in character description to allow reader projection
rubrics_metrics.description: "Make the fellow nice... Let every woman reader picture him to herself as her particular man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately leave physical specifics vague (not tall/short, bearded/clean-shaven) so readers can supply their own ideal. The essay cites a friend who purposely uses vague description so each reader personalizes the hero, increasing engagement; this is offered as an intentional strategy rather than a failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid formulaic/repetitive plots and clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not live new stories—nor write them either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of and try to avoid recycled plot formulas and stock scenes (the drawing-room, the picnic, the moor rendezvous). The essay lampoons small changes (Robinson→Jones; Brighton→Eastbourne) that leave the story essentially the same. Anti-patterns include relying on familiar set-pieces (Duchess who says improper things, slangy girl, clergyman who imparts epigrams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-specify physical 'points' or use mechanical lists
rubrics_metrics.description: The days when we used to catalogue the heroine’s 'points' are past... 'Her eyes!' They were invariably deep and liquid... 'Her forehead!' It was always 'low and broad.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the mechanical laundry-listing of features (eyes, nose, forehead, chin, complexion) which produces cliché and boredom. The author ridicules the old practice of instructing readers how to 'work out' hair color or skin tone and suggests modern writers should not rely on such formulaic inventories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure scenes/chapters provide more than a sub-editor's synopsis
rubrics_metrics.description: The bright and intelligent sub-editor... had provided me with a short synopsis of those first six chapters, so that without the trouble of reading them I knew what they were all about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write chapters and episodes that contain moments, character depth, or originality that cannot be fully captured by a one-line synopsis. The danger illustrated: if serial summaries give all the salient points ('much smart talk is indulged in'), readers and editors may see the full text as redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine archetypal traits economically to appeal broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: He sees to it that his heroine has a bit of every girl in her. Generally speaking, she is a cross between Romola and Dora Copperfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical tactic is to blend recognizable qualities from successful archetypes to create a heroine with wide appeal, rather than inventing unnatural detail. This is presented as a commercial device (helps sales) rather than pure artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pretentious/obscure ornamental phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: If we desire to be exact we mention... an 'elusive expression,' or a penetrating fragrance... Or we say that she moved, the centre of an indefinable nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of using vague-sounding but empty ornaments (elusive expression, indefinable nuance, penetrating fragrance) that sound literary but convey little. Prefer clear, concrete imagery that actually communicates rather than pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of publishing/market/length economics
rubrics_metrics.description: We are paid by the length of our manuscript at rates from half-a-crown a thousand words, and upwards... How are we to live on novels the serial rights of which to most of us will work out at four and nine-pence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how serialization, payment-per-word, and editorial condensation affect how you should structure and lengthen (or tighten) your work. The essay warns authors to be practical about living from writing and about trends toward ever-shorter published instalments.
